content: When a mother chooses replacement feeding, it is important to provide guidance on managing breast discomfort. The breasts may feel uncomfortable for a while, so it is recommended to avoid stimulating them. Support the breasts with a well-fitting bra or cloth, but do not bind them tightly, as this can increase discomfort. Applying a compress can help; some mothers find warmth soothing, while others prefer a cold compress to reduce swelling. Teach the mother to express just enough milk to relieve discomfort, which can be done a few times a day if the breasts are overly full. However, this should not be done if it causes discomfort, and the amount expressed should be less than what the baby would typically take to avoid stimulating increased milk production. Pain relief can be achieved with analgesics such as ibuprofen or paracetamol. Some women also use plant-based remedies, such as herbal teas or raw cabbage leaves applied directly to the breasts, to reduce pain and swelling. Advise the mother to seek medical care if the breasts become painful, swollen, red, or if she feels unwell or has a fever above 38°C. The delivery room should be warm, with a temperature of 25–28°C and no drafts. Immediately after birth, the baby should be dried thoroughly and placed on the mother’s abdomen or a warm, clean surface. Skin-to-skin contact is encouraged for at least two hours after birth, with the baby covered by a soft, dry cloth. If the mother cannot provide skin-to-skin contact due to complications, the baby should be wrapped in clean, dry, warm clothing and placed in a cot, covered with a blanket. A radiant warmer can be used if the room is not warm enough or if the baby is small. Explain to the mother the importance of keeping the baby warm to maintain health. Keep the baby close to the mother (rooming-in) and avoid separation unless necessary. Assess the baby’s warmth every four hours by touching the feet; if they are cold, use skin-to-skin contact, add extra blankets, and reassess. Keep the room warm, and if it is not sufficiently warm, always cover the baby with a blanket or use skin-to-skin contact. At home, explain to the mother that babies need one more layer of clothing than adults or older children. Keep the room or part of the room warm, especially in cold climates. During the day, dress or wrap the baby appropriately, and at night, let the baby sleep with the mother or within easy reach to facilitate breastfeeding. Avoid placing the baby on cold or wet surfaces, and do not bathe the baby immediately after birth. After bathing, dry the baby thoroughly and keep them warm. Avoid tight swaddling, as it can make the baby cold. For small babies, maintain a room temperature of at least 25°C with no drafts. Encourage the mother to keep the baby in skin-to-skin contact as much as possible and use extra clothing, socks, a cap, and blankets to keep the baby warm when not in contact with the mother. If bathing is necessary, do so in a warm room with warm water, and dry the baby immediately and thoroughly afterward. Seek medical care if the baby’s feet remain cold after rewarming. For cord care, wash hands before and after handling the cord. Do not apply anything to the stump, and fold the diaper below the stump to keep it clean and dry. Cover the stump loosely with clean clothing, and if it becomes soiled, wash it with clean water and soap, then dry it thoroughly. If the umbilicus becomes red, drains pus, or bleeds, examine the baby and manage accordingly. Advise the mother to seek care if these signs occur. Do not bandage the stump or abdomen, and avoid applying substances or medicines to the stump. Minimize unnecessary handling of the stump. For sleeping, use a bed net during the day and night to protect the baby. Let the baby sleep on their back or side, and keep them away from smoke or people who are smoking. Regarding hygiene, at birth, only remove blood or meconium from the baby’s skin and do not remove the vernix. Delay bathing for at least six hours after birth. Later, wash the baby’s face, neck, and underarms daily, and clean the buttocks when soiled, ensuring they are dried thoroughly. Bathe the baby only when necessary, ensuring the room is warm and there are no drafts. Use warm water for bathing, and dry the baby thoroughly before dressing and covering them. For breastfeeding, counsel the mother on the importance of exclusive breastfeeding during pregnancy and after birth. Breast milk contains the exact nutrients a baby needs, is easily digested, and protects against infections. Babies should start breastfeeding within one hour of birth and should not receive any other food or drink before breastfeeding. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life. Breastfeeding supports the baby’s development and strengthens the bond between mother and baby. It can also help delay a new pregnancy. Encourage the mother to initiate breastfeeding within one hour of birth, keeping the baby in skin-to-skin contact on her chest. Look for signs of readiness to breastfeed, such as the baby looking around, opening their mouth, or searching. Let the baby release the breast on their own before offering the second breast. If the baby does not feed within one hour, examine the baby and reassess later. If the mother is ill and unable to breastfeed, help her express breast milk and feed the baby by cup. If breastfeeding is not possible, consider donated heat-treated breast milk or commercial infant formula as alternatives. Explain that her milk is the best food for the baby and is especially important for small babies. Small babies may feed less effectively at first, but breastfeeding will become easier as the baby grows. Encourage skin-to-skin contact to facilitate breastfeeding. Feed the baby every 2–3 hours, waking them if necessary. Always start with breastfeeding before offering expressed milk by cup. Allow the baby to feed for as long as needed, even with pauses. If the baby is not feeding well, express breast milk into the baby’s mouth or feed by cup. Teach the mother to observe swallowing when giving expressed milk. Start feeding one baby at a time until breastfeeding is well established.
